title: ITU INTERVIEWS @ GSR-26: Gift Kallisto Machengete, Director General, POTRAZ, Zimbabwe
transcriptText:
Welcome to GSR [music] 26, the Global
Symposium for Regulators. We're very
pleased to be joined in the studio today
by Mr. Gift Kalista Machingauta, who is
director of the General Postal and
Telecommunications Regulatory Authority
of Zimbabwe. And Mr. Machingauta,
welcome to the studio. Thank you.
Thank you for having me. Now, let me
start off by asking you a little bit
about GSR 26 and the other GSRs that you
may have attended. Why is this event
important to you?
Oh, thank thank you very much. Um yes, I
have attended a
number of
these meetings since 2016.
Um what I have,
you know, realized and
the benefits we have managed to get from
attendance have been the fact that
this is the meeting where regulators
meet.
Individually,
regulators may not have that clout to
regulate effectively.
Especially now that technology is
galloping, you know, and regulation is
following, you know, behind. We have AI.
How do we regulate AI?
I think
in in Uganda,
one regulator needs to suggest that in
order to regulate AI, we need to use AI.
So that AI regulates AI.
>> Mhm. So that only shows the problems
that regulators have in terms of, you
know, balancing
innovation
because you we need to allow technology
to to for for for economies to prosper.
We need to balance now
innovation and we have to regulate that
innovation so that technology is for the
betterment of humanity and does not harm
humanity.
So, when the regulators come together,
they discuss these issues and see best
practices in order to regulate properly.
And coming to the current
>> [clears throat]
>> uh GSR 202026
for us it has actually been an
eye-opener.
Why? Because
we have been presented with the best
practice guidelines.
And we believe that those best practice
guidelines can really assist us in you
know creating digital markets.
For Zimbabwe, we are looking at
GDP of 5% growth for 2026
and we believe that with the best
practice guidelines,
with the
you know drive towards a digital
markets, we might actually achieve that
level of economic development.
Yeah, it's not only the best practice
guidelines.
We were also presented with
the global
economic model and
and study Mhm. which is an economic an
econometric model. And using that
econometric model being popularized by
ITU, we believe that we can actually
manage to get stakeholders together, sit
on one table and you know if like
a whole of government approach so that
we determine exactly where we can put
our investments.
It is known that
digital transformation is only one of
the many sectors in a country.
So we are always competing for you know
funding. We are competing for investment
but to be able to convince the powers
that be that we need investment in
broadband we need we have to be able to
show the impact that will come out of
such investments and this impact should
be impact that develops or impact that
enhances
humanity that improves human lives. That
is the impact that we to to achieve. Let
me ask you what is the digital landscape
look like currently in Zimbabwe at the
moment?
Yes
in in Zimbabwe we are
a developing country to begin with.
So we have
been pushing for digitization.
For example
we realized that there was
a huge digital divide
between
towns and the rural areas and most of
our people are actually in the rural
areas.
So they were being left behind.
So we made a conscious
decision
to then move into those rural areas
and create digital centers there.
These digital centers would be centers
of excellency
where we provide government services
digitally.
Where we can have a telemedicine so that
people don't have to go to towns.
You know, [clears throat] they they they
will have these centers near them. And
if they are maybe
producing commodities, they can also
even go into e-commerce using these
digital centers.
We have also been doing a lot in terms
of e-learning.
Whereby we have been equipping schools,
creating
school computer laboratories so that
our, you know, students are not left
behind. We do have challenges, of
course,
to do with power, with electricity,
especially in the rural areas. But we
have started using solar energy
to power such,
you know, places. And and
>> satellite communication as well.
We actually licensed the Starlink.
Right. And right now they are
now over 80,000 subscribers for Starlink
in Zimbabwe. And mostly
in the rural areas, you know, the rural
schools, the rural clinics.
Which
which did not have connectivity. Now
they do have connectivity because of,
you know, satellite.
What's
What is the What are the main priorities
for you as a regulator in Zimbabwe?
Right now
the main
uh, priority
is implementation of our, um,
artificial intelligence strategy because
we launched an artificial intelligence
strategy.
So, it's the implementation of that
strategy. So, that we can, you know,
drive
artificial intelligence and gain from
use cases of, you know, which are being
brought by, you know,
technology.
Um, the other, uh,
important,
uh,
issue for for us
is to do with affordability.
Because there is no need to have the
technology which people cannot afford.
Sure. So, affordability is, uh, is an
issue.
Uh, we would want to provide affordable,
uh, internet, affordable connectivity.
And this is why we are
calling on investors to come. Um, we
have been talking to other, you know,
investors,
satellite investors, actually. So, that
when when they come, and we have many of
them, we hope that the price, the the
price of our connectivity actually goes
down and our people can, you know,
afford, including those people in the
rural areas. To benefit all. And I just
wanted to ask you, in terms of the
conversations that you've been hearing,
the themes that have been emerging, I
know that we've talked about AI, have
there been any others that have,
uh, struck you as particularly for this
year?
Yes, sure.
The the issue to do with, uh,
data.
Um,
uh,
how to collect, you know, uh authentic
data,
data with integrity,
which data we can feed into, you know,
systems,
so that at the end of [clears throat]
the day,
the decisions that are made are made
from evidence-based
research, and evidence-based research
can only come about when you have good,
you know, data sets. And I thought that
was very, very, you know, important,
especially for developing countries,
because our data it would be scattered
all over, but it is important that we
harness this data, create data sets, and
with that, we can really make decisions
based on
proper, you know, data, and such
decisions would
really help us move forward.
Finally, I mean, we're here on the last
day of GSR. What do you hope will be the
key takeaways from this year's GSR?
Oh, the the the takeaway uh
from this um year's GSR would be,
firstly,
uh the collaboration,
the importance of collaboration.
so many uh regulators have been here.
But for this particular one, I have
noticed that we also have quite a lot of
other stakeholders. Indeed. So, when all
these stakeholders come together, it
means we are all at the table at the
same time.
And uh we at at one time I attended the
industry um meeting. Mhm. We we those in
industry and commerce were talking about
the their, you know, applications, their
products, and so on. And regulators were
sitting in there and we could now
understand that, "Wow, okay, this is
where they're coming from." And
we are there.
Previously, regulators would have their
meeting as regulators. They are having
their meeting over there, but so we
actually applaud ITU for bringing all of
us together, regulators, academia, um
politicians, everyone at the same table.
Because our objective is the same.
Moving forward together in the spirit of
collaboration. Exactly.
Well, Mr. Gifted Lister Machengete,
Director General of the Postal and
Telecommunication Regulatory Authority
Zimbabwe, POTRAZ,
thank you so much for joining us today
and we hopefully will look forward to
catching up with you again at another
one. You've been here, you've been
attending GSR for 10 years. I'm sure
you'll be here for plenty more. I I
will, definitely. Thank you very much
indeed.
>> Oh, thank you. Thank you so much. And if
you've enjoyed this interview, which I'm
sure you will have, then do check out
our other interviews on our YouTube
channel, uh podcast, wherever you get
your podcast from, and for further
information visit our website at
www.itu.int.
Thanks for tuning in.
